title: Effect of thermal adaptation on seasonal outdoor thermal comfort

findings.statement: Neutral temperatures differed between hot and cool seasons: 29.3°C SET* in hot season vs. 28°C SET* in cool season
findings.sample: Field interviews conducted outdoors in central Taiwan (Taichung, Yunlin, Chiayi) from winter 2004 to summer 2005
findings.quote: Substituting MTSV = 0 into Equations (1) and (2) yields the neutral temperatures for subjects; 29.3 and 28°C SET* in hot and cool seasons, respectively.
findings.scope_conditions: Hot-humid outdoor climate in central Taiwan
findings.stimulus_description: Seasonal variation in microclimate from December 2004 to September 2005
findings.mechanism: Thermal adaptation through seasonal acclimatization and behavioral adjustment

findings.statement: Preferred temperatures differed between seasons: 28.5°C SET* in hot season vs. 26.7°C SET* in cool season, a difference of 1.8°C
findings.sample: Field interviews conducted outdoors in central Taiwan
findings.quote: the preferred temperatures were 28.5 and 26.7°C SET*, respectively, with a difference of 1.8°C SET*
findings.stimulus_description: Seasonal contrast in outdoor thermal environment
findings.mechanism: Thermal adaptation and seasonal comfort expectations

findings.statement: Hot season: MTSV = 0.130 SET* - 3.814 (R² = 0.92). Linear relationship between SET* and thermal sensation in hot season.
findings.sample: Field interviews from FIOT project, hot season subset
instruments_used: SET* calculation from Ta, Tmrt, RH, v
findings.quote: Hot season: MTSV = 0.130 SET* - 3.814 with R² = 0.92
findings.scope_conditions: Central Taiwan, hot season outdoor conditions
findings.stimulus_description: Variation in outdoor thermal environment across temperature range in hot season
findings.mechanism: Physiological thermal sensation response to heat stress

findings.statement: Cool season: MTSV = 0.074 SET* - 2.066 (R² = 0.95). Linear relationship between SET* and thermal sensation in cool season.
findings.sample: Field interviews from FIOT project, cool season subset
findings.quote: Cool season: MTSV = 0.074 SET* - 2.066 with R² = 0.95
findings.scope_conditions: Central Taiwan, cool season outdoor conditions
findings.stimulus_description: Variation in outdoor thermal environment in cool season
findings.mechanism: Physiological response to thermal environment, moderated by seasonal adaptation

findings.statement: Air temperature (Ta) and mean radiant temperature (Tmrt) are strongly related to thermal perception. Ta and Tmrt together explain the variance in thermal sensation across seasons.
findings.sample: FIOT project outdoor surveys, both seasons
findings.quote: Analysis reveals that people's thermal perceptions were strongly related to the air temperature (Ta) and mean radiant temperature (Tmrt), and not significant to air speed and air humidity.
findings.scope_conditions: Outdoor thermal environments in central Taiwan
findings.stimulus_description: Natural variation in Ta and Tmrt across seasons
findings.mechanism: Heat balance and radiative heat exchange

findings.consequent: Relative contribution to thermal sensation variance
findings.statement: ANOVA analysis: Operative temperature contributes 75.7% to explained variance in TSV in hot season (p < 0.05)
findings.sample: FIOT outdoor survey respondents, hot season
findings.quote: Operative temperature 75.7** Vapour pressure 23.9* Wind speed 0.4
findings.mechanism: Thermal comfort dependence on heat balance

findings.consequent: Relative contribution to thermal sensation variance
findings.statement: ANOVA analysis: Operative temperature contributes 87.3% to explained variance in TSV in cool season (p < 0.001)
findings.sample: FIOT outdoor survey respondents, cool season
findings.mechanism: Thermal comfort strongly dependent on air/radiant temperature

findings.consequent: Relative contribution to thermal sensation variance
findings.statement: ANOVA: Vapour pressure contributes 23.9% in hot season (p < 0.05) and 12.1% in cool season (p < 0.05)
findings.mechanism: Evaporative cooling effectiveness varies with humidity and season

findings.consequent: Relative contribution to thermal sensation variance
findings.statement: ANOVA: Wind speed contributes only 0.4% in hot season and 0.5% in cool season - negligible contribution to thermal sensation variance
findings.scope_conditions: Central Taiwan outdoor, low wind speed region
findings.stimulus_description: Wind speed variation in subtropical Taiwan (average 0.8-1.2 m/s year-round)
findings.mechanism: Low average wind speeds in tropical region limit effect

findings.statement: Clothing insulation decreases with increasing temperature. In cool season at Ta ~14°C, clothing ~1.1 clo; in hot season at Ta ~28°C, clothing ~0.5 clo. Difference of 0.6 clo between seasons.
findings.quote: In the cool season, the mean clothing insulation value increased to 1.1 clo at a mean Ta of 14°C. In the hot season, the amount of clothing decreased to 0.5 clo at the corresponding Ta of 28°C.
findings.mechanism: Behavioral thermal adaptation through clothing adjustment

findings.antecedent: Season (hot vs. cool) combined with thermal index conditions
findings.statement: In hot season, ~100% prefer cooler at SET* >4°C; in cool season, ~100% prefer warmer at SET* <15°C. The temperature ranges showing preference divergence are 26.7°C (hot) and 28.5°C (cool).
findings.sample: Preference scale ratings from FIOT interviews
findings.quote: the preferred temperatures were 28.5 and 26.7°C SET*, respectively, with a difference of 1.8°C SET*
findings.scope_conditions: Outdoor thermal environments in central Taiwan
findings.stimulus_description: Seasonal variation in thermal environment at fixed locations
findings.mechanism: Seasonal thermal adaptation shifts preference distribution

findings.antecedent: Thermal sensation (TSV) divergence between heat-balance indices
findings.consequent: Explanation by thermal adaptation and psychological factors
findings.statement: Thermal preferences for Ta when experiencing identical SET* in two seasons diverged. Results show that thermal indices alone cannot fully explain thermal preferences; psychological and behavioral factors (thermal adaptation) are necessary.
findings.sample: Comparison of thermal preference responses to identical SET* in different seasons
findings.quote: people have different thermal preferences in different contexts, despite their having identical values of SET*. The results are thus suggesting that the thermal preferences for outdoor people cannot be completely explained by thermal indices based on the energy balance of the human body.
findings.scope_conditions: Central Taiwan, outdoor thermal comfort contexts
findings.stimulus_description: Same SET* values experienced in different seasonal contexts
findings.mechanism: Seasonal thermal adaptation modulates comfort expectations beyond physiological heat balance

limitations: Field study limited to central Taiwan (hot-humid subtropical region) - generalizability to other climate zones unclear
Small annual temperature range (~15°C variation) compared to temperate zones (28-31°C) - different adaptation dynamics may apply in higher-latitude regions
Wind speed variation negligible in study region (0.8-1.2 m/s year-round) - wind effects may differ in windier climates
Data collection limited to 2004-2005; temporal stability of adaptation effects not assessed
Humidity preference findings suggest VP matters only during high-humidity conditions (>35°C VT); applicability to dry climates unknown
Sample composition and demographics not fully specified
No assessment of acclimatization timescale or rate of adaptation
overall_theory_links: thermal_adaptation_theory: Central thesis that seasonal thermal adaptation shifts neutral and preferred temperatures
heat_balance_physiology: MTSV regression on SET* demonstrates dominant role of operative temperature in thermal sensation
behavioral_adaptation: Seasonal clothing adjustment (0.6 clo difference) exemplifies behavioral response to thermal conditions
contextual_comfort_framework: Finding that identical SET* yields different preferences in different seasons supports contextual comfort models
expectation_theory: Seasonal shifts in comfort expectations mediate preference formation beyond physiological indices

key_methodological_notes.study_design: Field survey with concurrent microclimate measurements
key_methodological_notes.sample_recruitment: 8077 data sets collected across three locations (Taichung, Yunlin, Chiayi); 1644 outdoor interviews analyzed
key_methodological_notes.measurement_approach: Concurrent physical (Ta, Tmrt, RH, v) and subjective (TSV, preference, sensation) measurements using standardized instruments
analysis_techniques: ANOVA variance decomposition (relative contributions of microclimatic parameters)
key_methodological_notes.data_quality: ISO 7726 compliant measurements; ASHRAE standardized sensation scale
